description: Science and pet enthusiasts interested in interdisciplinary solutions to issues that matter to all of us.
summary: Afghanistan’s Qosh Tepa Canal is a 285-km unlined irrigation canal built to expand the country’s agricultural capacity, but independent information about its progress and environmental impact is scarce. Qosh Tepa Radar Pulse is a proof-of-concept web tool that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band SAR imagery (HH and HV polarizations) to monitor changes along the canal. By comparing two acquisitions (June 22 and October 20, 2026), it highlights localized moisture and roughness anomalies that can indicate water seepage and groundwater accumulation, which lead to soil salinization and undermine the canal’s own goal of improving farmland. Because NISAR data is open and can be verified by any party, the tool offers an objective, neutral view of a region with limited ground access. In the future, we plan to use NISAR’s 12-day repeat cycle to turn this into a reliable instrument for continuous, multilateral observation of the canal.
details:
What it does: An interactive web application and geospatial pipeline that compares two NISAR L-band SAR acquisitions (June 22 and October 20, 2026) along the Qosh Tepa Canal. It includes a split-screen HH/HV slider, a calibrated change-detection layer (“Where did it change?”) that isolates local moisture and roughness anomalies from broad regional trends, a 5-step guided walkthrough, and a SAR physics explainer with scientific guardrails on what radar can and cannot measure.

How it works: We processed NISAR L2 GCOV granules in Python (GDAL, h5py, NumPy) and QGIS, then built a front end with Leaflet.js on an Esri World Imagery basemap. HH reflects surface scattering (soil moisture), and HV reflects volumetric scattering (vegetation and roughness).

Why it matters: Afghanistan’s government is largely closed to outside observers, so satellite data is the most reliable way to follow what happens along the canal. NISAR data is open, so any party can verify it. The canal’s progress is limited by outdated technology and a lack of financial and technical resources, not a lack of interest. Objective, public data benefits Afghanistan too: water seeping into the soil and excess groundwater cause soil salinization, which degrades the land the canal is meant to irrigate. The canal also affects downstream water security for Central Asia.

Limitations: This is a proof-of-concept. We compared only two time points because we could not process more scenes during the hackathon. The imagery is not a proof but a screening indicator for field observation. Tried to compare two 2026 NISARs with 2023 Sentinel-1 picture using QGIS, but were not able to process Sentinel-1 because it was too time-consuming for a given period of time considering we are beginner users of satellite and radar signal data.

Creativity and next steps: We turn complex radar backscatter into insights for water managers and policymakers, in a transparent and verifiable form that is easy to understand and makes sense of with the help of storytelling elements such as the snake diagram and meaningful insights such as the policy evidence deck. There is also an interactive “What does the radar see?” tool that contains visual and text explanations of how the radar signals backscatter off of 4 different surface types, how the backscatter patterns appear on the images and how we can interpret them. The tool helps general public and decision-makers that are not familiar with radar imagery to make meaningful insights. Next, we will use NISAR’s 12-day repeat cycle for continuous time-series monitoring combining them with precipitation measurements, as a trusted tool for multilateral observation of the region.

Tools: VS Code, Python (GDAL, h5py, NumPy), QGIS, Esri World Imagery, Leaflet.js, https://search.asf.alaska.edu/#/ : NISAR_L2_PR_GCOV_033_121_D_070_4005_DHDH_A_20261020T142732_20261020T142805_P05023_N_F_J_001.h5 NISAR_L2_PR_GCOV_023_121_D_070_4005_DHDH_A_20260622T142734_20260622T142809_P05023_N_F_J_001.h5
